title: Activepieces vs IFTTT: Workflow Automation Compared
summary: Activepieces vs IFTTT differ in pricing, automation triggers, and integrations available. See which platform matches your technical skill level and budget.
body_markdown:
## Which tool fits multi-step business workflows


When a workflow has branches, loops and a team that must maintain it, a team-owned workflow platform fits, and **unlimited flows on every plan, free included** , mean the team isn't rationing them.


IFTTT is built around one trigger leading to an action, which is the right shape for a single rule and a narrow one for a process.


### Workflow logic and error handling compared


Read an IFTTT applet and you see one condition and its result. Paid tiers add more than one action and some filtering, but the model stays a rule rather than a flow.


Business processes need more. A lead has to go down one path or another, line items need a loop, a code step may have to reshape a payload, and something must decide what happens when the CRM call fails.


A platform that charges 1 credit per flow run however many steps it holds makes a ten-step flow with branches, a loop and a code step cost the same as the two-step workaround it replaced.


Zapier's per-task billing works the other way, and pricing that rises with every step taxes the builder for splitting work into smaller, safer integrations. Here the run is the meter, not the steps inside it.


The limit is that you now own the logic, so someone has to design and test it.


### Team access, SSO and self-hosting


Where it runs is the first question. IFTTT is a hosted consumer service, so every run crosses the public internet and there's no self-hosted option. If your CRM or database sits behind a restricted network, that settles the question before features come up.


If you deploy the platform inside your own infrastructure, including through Docker, **flows reach internal systems without leaving your perimeter** . Its community edition is open source under the MIT licence, which means you can read the code you run.


Admin controls and SSO sit on higher plans, and the enterprise self-hosted setup is arranged through sales rather than self-serve.


### Building workflows with conditional branches


Picture the canvas below as a real process. A lead arrives from the CRM, an AI step qualifies it, a condition splits qualified from unqualified, and each side continues with its own actions, such as a record write, a team notification and an email.


On the canvas, each step is visible, ordered and editable by anyone on the team with access. That's what makes the flow something the team owns rather than a rule one person set up.


The limits are real: a flow this size needs a named owner, review when connected systems change, and a decision on where it's hosted.
